forces.title: Private capital surge meets global infrastructure investment needs.
forces.description: Global infrastructure fundraising reached a record of nearly $200 billion in 2025, surpassing the previous high. Limited partners are increasingly allocating to infrastructure, viewing it as the leading asset class for diversification and performance. This influx of private capital is critical to meeting the estimated $106 trillion global infrastructure investment needed by 2040, enabling long-term economic growth.
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: Expanding infrastructure definition attracts diverse private capital investments.
forces.description: The concept of infrastructure is broadening beyond traditional assets like roads and power grids to include data centers, charging stations, and fiber-optic networks. This evolving landscape attracts private capital to new verticals and intersecting sectors, with energy, digital, and telecom capturing an outsized share of recent infrastructure deals (approximately 75% by value in 2025).
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: Limited partners increase infrastructure allocations for diversification and returns.
forces.description: A McKinsey survey indicates 51% of global LPs plan to increase infrastructure allocations over the next three years, making it the leading asset class for intended increases. Diversification (68%) and expected return improvements (52%) are primary motivations, highlighting infrastructure's growing strategic importance within private market portfolios and ensuring continued capital flow into the sector.
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: Infrastructure investors shift towards higher-risk, value-added strategies.
forces.description: The infrastructure sector is maturing, with investors increasingly willing to move up the risk curve from "traditional core" to "core plus" and "value added" categories. These higher-risk strategies, which include greenfield and brownfield projects and assets requiring turnarounds, saw significant fundraising growth (core plus up 390%, value added up 30%), reflecting a pursuit of higher returns as the market evolves.
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: Lengthening holding periods challenge infrastructure investment liquidity and returns.
forces.description: Infrastructure investment capital cycles are trending longer, with the average age of holdings increasing from 3.1-3.3 years (2017-22) to 3.5-3.8 years (2023-24). This elongation, coupled with declining distributions to paid-in capital (DPI hitting a record low of ~13% in 2025), is intensifying liquidity pressures for limited partners and making it more difficult to realize distributions in shorter timeframes.
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: Higher debt costs and asset multiples pressure traditional IRR targets.
forces.description: Internal Rate of Return (IRR) targets, a primary metric for LPs and GPs, face mounting pressure from two key factors: a higher cost of debt (exceeding 2009-2020 levels) and elevated public and private multiples that drive up purchase prices for infrastructure assets. This combination makes achieving traditional return expectations more challenging for infrastructure investors.
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: Active value creation and advanced technology drive future infrastructure returns.
forces.description: As market tailwinds alone become insufficient, return drivers are shifting from multiples expansion and financial structuring to operational performance and capital productivity. Managerial excellence and leveraging advanced technologies, particularly AI for asset-performance-focused use cases like generative scheduling and site identification, are becoming critical for generating true alpha and improving capital efficiency, especially for greenfield projects.
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: European airports face heightened investor caution due to structural pressures.
forces.description: European airports are experiencing significant structural pressures including moderating traffic growth (2.0-2.5% annually vs 5% pre-pandemic), unit revenue pressures from low-cost carriers, rising operating costs (1% above inflation), and increasing capital intensity (CapEx per passenger projected to rise ~80% by 2043). These dynamics have led investors to become more cautious, adding hurdles to financing new infrastructure projects.
forces.source_title: European Airports Add New Routes to Value Creation

forces.title: Digitalization and AI enhance airport operational efficiency and capacity utilization.
forces.description: Over 90% of large European airports are prioritizing digital transformation to boost efficiency, expand capacity within existing infrastructure, and reduce operating expenses. Initiatives like optimized gate allocation, dynamic parking pricing, AI-enabled passenger flow monitoring, and predictive maintenance are unlocking latent capacity and improving service quality, contributing up to 3 percentage points of EBITDA improvement and making assets more attractive for investment.
forces.source_title: European Airports Add New Routes to Value Creation

forces.title: Airport non-aeronautical revenue growth offsets declining aeronautical charges.
forces.description: Almost half of European airports are rethinking commercial strategies to boost non-aeronautical revenues per passenger by 5-10% over the next decade. This strategy aims to counteract downward pressure on aeronautical charges by strengthening food & beverage offerings, revamping retail formats, introducing omnichannel retail, personalized offers, and exploring new revenue streams like solar farms and onsite energy hubs, enhancing asset profitability.
forces.source_title: European Airports Add New Routes to Value Creation

forces.title: Unclear aviation Net Zero policy impedes investor risk assessment for airports.
forces.description: The UK Government's lack of a robust policy framework to ensure the aviation sector reaches Net Zero by 2050 creates significant commercial risks for airport operators and, consequently, for investors. Without clear and funded policies for sustainable aviation fuels and engineered removals, investors cannot accurately assess long-term aviation demand and the associated risks of airport expansions, hindering investment decisions.
forces.source_title: Advice to the UK Government on proposed Heathrow Airport expansion

forces.title: Aviation decarbonisation costs reflected in ticket prices may moderate demand.
forces.description: To achieve Net Zero in aviation, the 'polluter pays' principle suggests reflecting decarbonisation costs in ticket prices. This would fund sustainable aviation fuels and engineered removals while managing demand growth. Estimated ticket price increases could be substantial (e.g., £150 for a return trip to Alicante by 2050), potentially moderating demand and impacting revenue forecasts for airport infrastructure.
forces.source_title: Advice to the UK Government on proposed Heathrow Airport expansion

viewpoints.title: European airports face investment hurdles despite enduring private capital appeal.
viewpoints.description: Structural changes, including moderating traffic growth, unit revenue pressures, rising operating costs, and increasing capital intensity, are challenging the operating environment for European airports. These dynamics are weighing on the sector’s economics and its ability to attract investment. Investors have grown more cautious towards airports, adding hurdles to financing infrastructure projects, despite private capital markets continuing to view airports as core infrastructure assets with long-term appeal.
viewpoints.source_title: European Airports Add New Routes to Value Creation

viewpoints.title: Private capital surge drives global infrastructure investment with record fundraising.
viewpoints.description: Private capital is increasingly pivotal in meeting the world’s growing infrastructure needs, with global fundraising reaching a record nearly $200 billion in 2025. Limited partners consistently prioritize infrastructure for increased allocations, citing both diversification and performance. This substantial inflow of private capital is seen as a critical enabler for long-term economic growth and addressing the extensive global infrastructure requirements through 2040.
viewpoints.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

viewpoints.title: Infrastructure investors shift to higher-risk, higher-return strategies as market matures.
viewpoints.description: As the infrastructure sector matures and investors seek higher returns, there is a clear willingness to move up the risk curve. Fundraising for 'core plus' and 'value added' categories saw significant growth, while 'core' declined. This indicates a shift towards investments in greenfield and brownfield projects, or acquisitions requiring operational turnarounds, signaling a more active and sophisticated approach to capital deployment in infrastructure.
viewpoints.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

viewpoints.title: Lengthening investment holding periods challenge liquidity for infrastructure capital.
viewpoints.description: Infrastructure capital cycles are extending, with the average age of holdings increasing from 3.1-3.3 years in 2017-2022 to 3.5-3.8 years in 2023-2024. This trend, combined with Distributions to Paid-in Capital (DPI) hitting its lowest recorded level in 2025, intensifies liquidity pressures for limited partners. Such extended holding periods necessitate robust value creation strategies to maintain investor returns amidst tightening market conditions.
viewpoints.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

viewpoints.title: Active value creation and AI adoption are crucial for future infrastructure returns.
viewpoints.description: The infrastructure market is evolving beyond passive investing, requiring managers to actively generate alpha. Return drivers are shifting from financial structuring to operational performance and capital productivity. Leveraging advanced technologies, particularly AI, for asset-performance-focused use cases such as generative scheduling and site identification, is becoming essential to improve capital efficiency and deliver robust returns, especially for greenfield projects and complex business models.
viewpoints.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

viewpoints.title: Robust Net Zero policy framework essential for aviation investor risk assessment.
viewpoints.description: The UK Government must provide a robust policy framework for the aviation sector to reach Net Zero by 2050. This is crucial for investors to properly assess the commercial risks associated with airport expansions and long-term demand. Without clear policies on funding and financing for sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) and engineered removals, the uncertainty impedes adequate risk evaluation by investors in aviation infrastructure.
viewpoints.source_title: Advice to the UK Government on proposed Heathrow Airport expansion

demand_drivers.description: Increasing global population drives demand for all types of infrastructure.
Parabolic technological advancement necessitates new and upgraded infrastructure, particularly in digital and energy sectors.
The shift towards renewable energy sources requires significant investment in energy and power infrastructure.
Power demand is expected to increase by more than 3% a year in some regions, requiring substantial grid and generation investment.
Nearly $7 trillion in data center investment may be needed through 2030 to keep pace with demand for compute power, highlighting digital infrastructure needs.

market_sizing.methodology: Estimated cumulative global infrastructure investment required through 2040 for traditional assets (roads, ports, bridges, power grids) and next-generation assets (data centers, charging stations, fiber-optic networks). Energy and digital sectors account for about 40% of this total.
market_sizing.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

demand_drivers.description: 51% of global LPs plan to increase infrastructure allocations over the next three years, driven by diversification and performance.
Infrastructure is outpacing other private-market categories in fundraising growth.

market_sizing.methodology: Global closed-end infrastructure fundraising volume, reaching a new high. Preceded by $126 billion in 2024 and $95 billion in 2023.
market_sizing.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

demand_drivers.description: Capital deployment is better at keeping up with fundraising, leading to a reduction in unallocated funds.

pnl_drivers.description: In previous decades, LP demand outpaced deal supply, contributing to fund fragmentation and higher dry powder levels.

market_sizing.methodology: Infrastructure dry powder as a percentage of Assets Under Management (AUM). This figure has nearly halved from the prior decade’s highs of around 40% (2009-2017).
market_sizing.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth
